What mir_compile() accepts

Source: vignettes/mir-compile.Rmd
mir-compile.Rmd
library(zumir)

mir_compile() compiles an R function written in a small numeric subset of R. Its promise is simple: the compiled function returns exactly what R returns, bit for bit, or it errors. It never gives a different answer. Where matching R would not be cheap, it refuses: at compile time when the function itself is the problem, at the call when an argument is.

The subset

Arguments are doubles without attributes. One that is indexed (x[i]), passed to length() or to seq_along() is a vector; any other that the body reads must have length one. An argument the body never reads is never evaluated, as in R. Arguments have no defaults, there is no ..., and the body never assigns to one.

Locals are double or logical scalars, for loop counters, and double vectors made by one y <- numeric(size) at the top of the body, changed only by y[i] <- value.

Code: {, <-, =, if/else, while, for over seq_len(n), seq_along(x) and a:b (counting down when a > b), break, next, return().

Operations: + - * / ^ %% %/%, unary -, comparisons, !, && and || with R’s three-valued logic; exp, log, log1p, expm1, sqrt, abs, floor, ceiling, trunc, sin, cos, tan; two-argument min and max; length, is.na, is.nan, is.finite, as.double.

The result is a double scalar, or a vector local.

csum <- mir_compile(function(x) {
  y <- numeric(length(x))
  acc <- 0
  for (i in seq_along(x)) {
    acc <- acc + x[i]
    y[i] <- acc
  }
  y
})
csum(c(1, 2, NA, 4))
#> [1]  1  3 NA NA

Where it errors and R would not

Each of these is a place where R gives an answer the compiled code could only match at a cost, so it errors instead.

R mir_compile() Why
x[0], x[length(x) + 1], x[NA], x[1.5] read numeric(0), NA, the truncated index an error none of them is the element at that index
seq_len(2.5) and numeric(2.5) truncate; 1.5:3 steps from 1.5 an error a size or bound must be a whole number
integer arithmetic past .Machine$integer.max gives NA with a warning an error the loop counter is a machine integer
an integer, logical or character argument computes in its own type an error the compiled code computes in doubles
an argument with names, dim or a class keeps or dispatches on them an error the compiled code sees only the numbers
a scalar argument of length 0 or 3 recycles an error it is used as one number 
first <- mir_compile(function(x) x[1])
first(numeric())
#> Error:
#> ! subscript out of bounds, NA or not a whole number

And at compile time, each with its reason:

Refused Why
a call to any other function, <<-, repeat, strings, lists outside the subset
a result R would type as integer or logical (length(x), a > b, abs(i) of a counter) R would return an integer or logical; write as.double()
exp or + rebound in the function’s environment the compiled code keeps base R’s meaning
a local with the name of a function the body calls R would look the function up past the local
a default, ..., or an assignment to an argument R’s lazy defaults and copies are not modelled
numeric() inside a loop or branch, z <- y, a second numeric() for one name R’s copy-on-modify is not modelled
a local that may be read before it is assigned R would error, or not, depending on the path
the loop variable read after its loop R leaves it at the last value, or NULL
min(x) or max(a, b, c) only two-argument min and max are supported 
mir_compile(function(x) sum(x))
#> Error:
#> ! mir_compile(): `sum` is not in the subset in `sum(x)`.

Warnings

Where R warns, the compiled function gives the same warning: “NaNs produced” from log(-1) or sqrt(-1), and “probable complete loss of accuracy in modulus” from %%. It gives each once per call, where a loop in R may warn many times.

NA and NaN together

Where an NA and a NaN meet in one operation, R leaves open which comes out (see ?NA), and so does mir_compile(): the answer can differ between R, the two tiers and different builds. is.na() is TRUE either way, but is.nan() of such a value can take a different branch.

Interrupts

Every loop counts its iterations, and every 2^16 of them checks for an interrupt. So Ctrl-C and setTimeLimit() stop a compiled loop, as they do an R one, with R’s own condition.

spin <- mir_compile(function(a) {
  s <- 0
  while (TRUE) s <- s + a
  s
})
setTimeLimit(elapsed = 1, transient = TRUE)
spin(1)
#> Error: reached elapsed time limit

cfunction() code is the user’s own C and is not interrupted.
